confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand descriptions agree (0 state the same rule, 2 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: Guy, J.B.M. (1974). A Grammar of the Northern Dialect of Sakao. Pacific Linguistics, Series B, No. 33. Canberra: Australian National University.
catalog_quote: 1.3. STRESS 1.3.1. Primary stress occurs either on the last word-final syllable to occur before the part of the phrase affected by phrase-final intonation, or on the last syllable of the phrase. 1.3.2. Secondary stress occurs on the final syllable of words, unless this final syllable contains the vowel ɨ, in which case it occurs on the penultimate. Monosyllabic particles, however, are most often unstressed, except in careful, slow speech. 1.3.3. Stress is realised as loudness and length of the vowel it affects, primary stress being louder than secondary stress. ... [p. 13, vowel chart:] VOWELS ... Central ... High close ... ɨ [ɨ]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Page header reads '78 – Benjamin Touati'; footnote 2 at the foot of the page reads exactly 'In Sakao, the stressed syllable is the last syllable of the word.' (decoded the text layeragrees). The footnote is anchored in section 2.1 body text: 'If V is an open-mid vowel then $- is the corresponding close-mid vowel. This is because there is no opposition between open-mid and close-mid vowel in unstressed syllables:2' — so the neutralisation claim is also verbatim. Section 1 (printed p. 77) fixes the variety: Wanohe, ca. 3,500 speakers, NE tip of Espiritu Santo, dialects Sakao (north, 1,500) and Nkep (south, 2,000); data collected by the author at Port Olry 2010-2012; earlier description Guy 19…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Sakao (qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule field; this footnote supplies a placement (final syllable) and a stress-conditioned vowel neutralisation. It is by the same author as the closed 2014 thesis and describes the same variety (Sakao dialect of Wanohe, Port Olry data).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable of the word. Same page, body text: "there is no opposition between open-mid and close-mid vowel in unstressed syllables", i.e. mid-vowel height contrasts are neutralised outside the stressed (final) syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: none mentioned; the statement is a one-line footnote in a morphology paper, not a phonology section
new_statements.identity_note: Touati's data are from the Sakao dialect of Wanohe (northern dialect, ca. 1,500 speakers, village of Port Olry, NE Espiritu Santo); the southern dialect Nkep (ca. 2,000 speakers) is treated by him as a dialect of the same language, and his stress footnote is explicitly about Sakao. Earlier description is Guy 1974 (not among the listed works, not opened).

tone_statements.citation: Guy, J. B. M. (1972). A grammar of the northern dialect of Sakao, a Melanesian language of Espiritu Santo (New Hebrides). Australian National University. 150 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Intonation 1.2 Except for the parts affected by expressive or phrase-final intonation, the pitch of a phrase is level. … 1.4 Phrase-final intonation is that of the last syllable or syllables of a phrase. Its pitch is level, but may be lower, or higher than, or level with that of the rest of the phrase. … 1.11 Stress is realized as loudness and length of the vowel it affects, primary stress being louder than secondary stress.

tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone described: pitch is level across the phrase apart from expressive and phrase-final intonation; word stress (final syllable) is realized as loudness and length, not pitch.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage (Guy 1974:12, 1.3.1-1.3.3) and the vowel chart (p.13) are verbatim in the PDF page scan we hold; p.17 additionally characterises ɨ as a very short underspecified central vowel, supporting the full-vs-reduced-vowel weight class and right edge. The record correctly takes Guy's word-level 'secondary stress' as word stress and his 'primary stress' as phrasal. (2) Deciding source is a 1974 published reference grammar (PL B-33), held in full. Glottolog lists one larger, newer description, Touati 2014 (588-pp. thesis), which is not openly accessible (theses.fr accessible=non, 403 on document). (3) downloaded the open Touati 2015 chapter (ANU SLIM 5): p.78 fn.2 says stress is on the last syllable of the word, confirming the right-edge/final default; it is silent on the ɨ exception and Touati's transcription uses clusters where Guy has ɨ, so under Touati's analys

tone.summary: Historical account of the Sakao twelve-vowel system; nothing on tone or pitch. States that stress is non-phonemic, on the last vowel, or on the penultimate when the last vowel is one specified vowel.
